corrected_value.authors: Kosinski, M., Bachrach, Y., Kasneci, G., Van Gael, J., & Graepel, T.
corrected_value.title: Crowd IQ: Measuring the intelligence of crowdsourcing platforms.

decisions.quote:
Our study aimed to replicate this study and test whether
(a) the impressive result stands with a larger base sample,
and (b) whether the estimated collective IQ based on crowdsourced answers exceeds the individual IQ of the contributing workers. In the Kosinski et al. (2012) study, sample size
effects were based on resampling a relatively limited set of
responses across several experimental conditions, which included manipulations of worker characteristics and reward
levels. We set out to replicate the key finding, using a simplified design to focus on the group size effect.
decisions.location: Section 1.2 (Introduction), page 92, lines 138-143 (and References, page 97, lines 755-758)
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly frames itself in its title, abstract, introduction, and discussion as a partial replication of Kosinski, Bachrach, Kasneci, Van Gael, & Graepel (2012), 'Crowd IQ: Measuring the intelligence of crowdsourcing platforms' (ACM WebSci 2012, DOI 10.1145/2380718.2380739). The competing match flag arose only because a second 2012 paper by the same five authors in different order (Bachrach et al., 2012, 'Crowd IQ: Aggregating opinions to boost performance', blind target_index 1) shares the 'Crowd IQ' title prefix. Shipped row 745 has Kosinski et al.'s exact author order and DOI, matching blind target_index 0.

decisions.quote:
Groups of at least 20 workers produce reliable and substantial gains in intelligence (90% CI = 114–132), equivalent to
performing at least 1 standard deviation above the population. Our findings thus largely corroborate the observations
of the original study, and – importantly – increase confidence
in the generality of the group size effect because we were able
sample without replacement from a large number of crowdsourced responses to generate virtual groups varying in size.
decisions.reason: Both shipped row 745 and blind target_index 0 code the outcome for Kosinski et al. (2012) as 'successful'. The authors explicitly state that their findings corroborate and replicate Kosinski et al.'s (2012) key finding that aggregating crowdsourced responses via majority vote yields substantial gains in collective IQ as group size increases with diminishing returns (despite a slightly smaller effect size). The secondary comparison of collective IQ against the best individual in the 50-worker subset (Section 3.3) is explicitly noted as an extension not in Kosinski et al. (2012) ('In contrast to the original study, this allowed us to conduct a direct comparison between individual intelligence and group intelligence', lines 612-613) that instead relates to Bachrach et al. (2012).

decisions.quote:
We examined the trade-off between the cost of response redundancy and the gain in output quality on the popular crowdsourcing platform Mechanical Turk, as a partial replication of Kosinski et al. (2012) who demonstrated a significant improvement in
performance by aggregating multiple responses through majority vote. We submitted single items from a validated intelligence
test as Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs) and aggregated the responses from “virtual groups” consisting of 1 to 24 workers.
decisions.reason: The study collected new data (8,093 crowdsourced responses from 221 unique Mechanical Turk workers completing Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices items) to re-test Kosinski et al.'s (2012) published finding. Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'replication'.
